snp2.1:0.2: This sutta is identical with Khp 6.
snp2.1:5.2: This appears to be equivalent to the liberation of immediacy mentioned in Thig 5:8, and the concentration that is the fruit of gnosis mentioned in AN 9:37.
snp2.1:8.1: An Indra pillar is a tall hardwood pillar planted at the entrance to a village. Similar analogies for the awakened mind appear at AN 6:55 and AN 9:26.
snp2.1:9.4: One who has reached this stage of practice will be reborn at most seven more times. See AN 3:88. On the danger of heedlessness even at this level of awakening, see SN 55:40.
snp2.1:10.4: These three qualities—identity-views, uncertainty, and attachment to habits and practices—are the fetters abandoned at the moment of first glimpsing unbinding, at stream-entry.
snp2.1:11.1: The four states of deprivation are rebirth as an animal, a hungry ghost, an angry demon, or a denizen of hell. In Buddhist cosmology none of these states is eternal.
snp2.1:11.2: The Sutta Nipāta commentary lists the six great wrongs as: murdering one’s mother, murdering one’s father, murdering an arahant, wounding a Buddha, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or choosing anyone other than a Buddha as one’s foremost teacher. The first five are listed in AN 5:129 as leading immediately to hell after death.
